cultivar: Seed-grown bushes brought from the south under the 1960s planting programme, plus Fuding Dabai, Longjing 43 and Zhongcha 108
processing: Pan-fired green: fired, rolled into curls and dried in rotating pans; some makers produce flat or needle styles, but the curled shape is the signature.
harvest_season: Open-air spring tea from late April into May (greenhouse tea from March); summer and autumn pickings follow, with autumn tea considered good value.
appearance_dry: Tight, curly, slightly fuzzy dark-green leaves, heavier and thicker-looking than southern greens.
appearance_wet: Thick, resilient leaves and buds, bright green, slow to tire.
taste_profile: Strong chestnut and roasted bean with a thick, savoury body, a slightly sharper edge than Laoshan and a sweet, durable finish across many steeps.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at 85 °C, or a tall glass brewed strong. Known for its staying power, so do not throw the leaves out after three steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by season within the current year: greenhouse spring tea from March, open-air spring tea from late April (the best and most expensive), then summer and autumn teas. Rizhao produces far more than Laoshan, so it is easy to find and good value; no pre-Qingming concept applies to the open-air crop. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Rizhao green is the other famous northern green, from the coast of southern Shandong a couple of hours down from Qingdao. Tea was established here in the mid-1960s under the same 'southern tea moves north' effort that planted Laoshan, and Rizhao has since become by far the larger producer: it is the everyday green of much of Shandong and increasingly of northern China.

The style is a pan-fired, tightly curled leaf. The bushes grow slowly through long, cold winters and a late spring, which makes the leaf thick, high in sugars and amino acids and remarkably resilient in the pot. Greenhouses give an early March crop; the open-air spring picking from late April is the one with the character.

In the cup it is strong and comforting: chestnut and roasted bean, a thick savoury body and a sweetness that lasts, with a slightly sharper edge than Laoshan. It is famous locally for lasting many steeps, and a gaiwan at 85 °C will get five or six out of it. It is a tea for a big glass and a long afternoon rather than a delicate tasting.

Buying: as with Laoshan, the questions are greenhouse or open-air, and which season. Spring open-air tea is the premium, autumn tea is the bargain with a softer, sweeter cup, and summer tea is the cheap, slightly coarse version. Volume is large, so there is no shortage and prices are moderate; the protected Rizhao origin label and a named district are the things to look for. Drink within the year.

It is a good green for cold brewing because of its sweetness and durability: ten grams in a litre of cold water for a few hours in the fridge.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. 'Mid-1960s' establishment date follows the usual account (1966 is commonly cited).
history:
Rizhao's tea is a planned transplant. Under the 'southern tea moves north' programme, the Beimenwai brigade was one of two pilot villages. In spring 1966 it planted 8.7 mu of tea, and 57 percent survived, which was counted as success at that latitude.

From there it grew into a large regional industry, and in 2013 Rizhao green tea was named among Shandong's top ten geographical indication trademarks.
